## Solution

**Yes, $\mu_f = \mu_g$.**

### Proof

Recall that the Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$ contains $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, the space of smooth compactly supported functions. Hence the hypothesis

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} h\,d\mu_f = \int_{\mathbb{R}} h\,d\mu_g \quad \text{for all } h \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$$

implies in particular

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}} \varphi\,d\mu_f = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \varphi\,d\mu_g \quad \text{for all } \varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}). \tag{1}$$

**Step 1: Extend to all of $C_c(\mathbb{R})$.**

The space $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ is uniformly dense in $C_c(\mathbb{R})$: given $\psi \in C_c(\mathbb{R})$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, by mollification there exists $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with $\|\psi - \varphi\|_\infty < \varepsilon$. Using (1) and the triangle inequality,

$$\left|\int \psi\,d\mu_f - \int \psi\,d\mu_g\right| \leq \left|\int (\psi - \varphi)\,d\mu_f\right| + \left|\int \varphi\,d\mu_f - \int \varphi\,d\mu_g\right| + \left|\int (\varphi - \psi)\,d\mu_g\right|.$$

The middle term vanishes by (1); the two outer terms are each bounded by $\varepsilon \cdot \mu_f(\mathbb{R}) = \varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon \cdot \mu_g(\mathbb{R}) = \varepsilon$ respectively, since $\mu_f, \mu_g$ are probability measures. Letting $\varepsilon \to 0$,

$$\int \psi\,d\mu_f = \int \psi\,d\mu_g \quad \text{for all } \psi \in C_c(\mathbb{R}). \tag{2}$$

**Step 2: Conclude $\mu_f = \mu_g$.**

A locally finite Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is uniquely determined by its action on $C_c(\mathbb{R})$ (this is the uniqueness part of the Riesz–Markov representation theorem: the linear functional $L(\psi) = \int \psi\,d\mu$ on $C_c(\mathbb{R})$ determines $\mu$). Both $\mu_f$ and $\mu_g$ are finite (hence locally finite) Borel measures on $\mathbb{R}$, and (2) says they define the same positive linear functional on $C_c(\mathbb{R})$. Therefore $\mu_f = \mu_g$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
